title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated images and videos of a real, named attorney were used to create fake social media profiles offering fraudulent immigration services. The failure did not originate inside a legitimate AI product deployment. Instead, it shows AI generation tools being used offensively, outside any sanctioned system, to manufacture convincing false identities at scale. The point of harm was the social media platforms, where thousands of fake profiles operated long enough to deceive paying victims before being detected and removed.

The scale of the operation, nearly 6,500 fake profiles across TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram, indicates that platform-level detection did not catch the profiles quickly. The fraud was discovered not by any automated system but by the real attorney noticing calls from deceived prospective clients. Removing the profiles required a hired anti-piracy company, meaning the burden of enforcement fell on the individual being impersonated rather than on the platforms hosting the content.

What is not established is who the scammers are, whether any of them have been identified or charged, and whether the payments victims made have been recovered or traced.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using AI-generated images of Leal to offer fraudulent immigration services, including false promises of US residency for $2,200. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, and the situation has dramatically worsened in recent months. An anti-piracy company hired by his office has removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scammers typically use social media videos directing victims to contact them via WhatsApp, where they send fake contracts and fake testimonials from supposed former clients. Leal warns consumers to be cautious of requests for payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App, emphasizing his office never requests payment over the phone. He plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams and urges immigrants to verify the identities of anyone offering legal services online.
